span.label: method
span.quote: We propose a simple, interpretable, and actionable framework for measuring and removing discrimination based on protected attributes.

span.label: discrimination against protected attributes in supervised learning
span.quote: As machine learning increasingly affects decisions in domains protected by anti-discrimination law, there is much interest in algorithmically measuring and ensuring fairness in machine learning.

span.label: system-or-tool-building
span.quote: We give a simple and effective framework for constructing classifiers satisfying our criterion from an arbitrary learned predictor.

span.label: the criterion is oblivious - it uses only joint statistics, not the interpretation of individual features
span.quote: it depends only on the joint statistics of the predictor, the target and the protected attribute, but not on interpretation of individual features

span.label: Satisfying the proposed oblivious criterion is not a proof of fairness (nor is violating it a proof of unfairness).
span.quote: Due to the limitations we described, satisfying our notion (or any other oblivious measure) should not be considered a conclusive proof of fairness.

span.label: The criterion requires reliable observed outcome labels, which are not always available and may themselves be biased.
span.quote: That said, having access to reliable “labeled data” is not always possible.

span.label: The near-optimality guarantee is relative to other constrained predictors only; the derived predictor need not be good in absolute terms.
span.quote: However, this does not mean that the predictor is necessarily good in an absolute sense.

span.label: No test of this kind can tell two situations apart, and the authors prove it about their own class of test.
span.quote: we pause to consider to what extent “black box” oblivious tests like ours can identify discriminatory predictions. To shed light on this issue, we introduce two possible scenarios for the dependency structure of the score, the target and the protected attribute. We will argue that while these two scenarios can have fundamentally different interpretations from the point of view of fairness, they can be indistinguishable from their joint distribution. In particular, no oblivious test can resolve which of the two scenarios applies

span.label: Access to the features does not rescue the test, without assumptions the authors decline to make.
span.quote: Without attaching meaning to the features or making causal assumptions about them, we do not gain any further insight on the two scores

span.label: Meeting the criterion can require deciding individual cases partly at random.
span.quote: This cannot be achieved with a single threshold for each group, but requires randomization

span.label: Who pays for the fairness is a property of the design, and the authors name the payer.
span.quote: The cost is thus born by the company using the classifier, which can decide to invest in better classification, rather than the classified group, which cannot

span.label: equal opportunity vs equalized odds - TWO CRITERIA, ONE STRICTLY WEAKER, AND THE PAPER PRICES THE GAP: equal opportunity relaxes equalized odds to the advantaged outcome group only, and in the case study equal opportunity keeps 92.8% of maximal profit against equalized odds' 80.2%, so a claim citing 'Hardt et al.' without saying which criterion is a claim about neither
span.quote: Equal opportunity is a weaker, though still interesting, notion of non-discrimination, and thus typically allows for stronger utility as we shall see in our case study

span.label: oblivious - IN A FORMAL SENSE THE PAPER DEFINES: a property is oblivious if it depends only on the joint distribution of target, protected attribute and prediction, which is what makes the criterion checkable from published statistics and also what makes it blind
span.quote: In line with other studies, our notion is oblivious: it depends only on the joint statistics of the predictor, the target and the protected attribute, but not on interpretation of individual features

span.label: demographic parity - THE CRITERION THIS ONE IS DEFINED AGAINST: it requires the decision to be independent of the protected attribute, which the authors reject because it forbids the perfectly accurate predictor and costs the most utility of the four thresholds they compare
span.quote: Demographic parity requires that a decision—such as accepting or denying a loan application—be independent of the protected attribute
